tldr:
Precision comes from **explicit criteria**, not from vague adjectives:

- **What to report:** bugs, security issues, comments whose claim **contradicts** the code.
- **What to skip:** style, naming, patterns the codebase already uses.
- **Severity levels:** each with a **concrete code example**.

“Be conservative” or “only high-confidence findings” don't cut false positives. When one category keeps producing false positives, **switch it off while you fix its criteria**, or developers stop trusting every finding. The docs' framing: write for a brilliant new colleague who doesn't know your norms.
mentalModel: Your reviewer is a brilliant new hire on day one. “Be careful” tells them nothing; a checklist of what to flag, what to ignore and what “critical” looks like tells them everything. And a smoke alarm that goes off every time you make toast gets its battery pulled — noisy categories cost trust in the accurate ones.
whatItIs:
The exam guide covers designing prompts with explicit criteria to improve precision and reduce false positives (Guide §6 ·
TS 4.1, p.16). The platform's prompting best practices give the general principle: be clear, direct and specific.

**Sub-concepts — each with its picture to remember**

| # | Sub-concept | 🧭 Mental model | ⭐ Exam reference |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Explicit criteria vs vague instructions | A checklist for a new hire, not “be careful”. | ⭐ TS 4.1 · Knowledge 1 |
| 2 | Confidence filters don't fix precision | A confident reviewer is confidently wrong about style. | ⭐ TS 4.1 · Knowledge 2 |
| 3 | Report / Skip categories | Two lists on the wall: flag these, ignore those. | ⭐ TS 4.1 · Skill 1 |
| 4 | Severity with examples | “Critical looks like this” beats “critical means very serious”. | ⭐ TS 4.1 · Skill 3 |
| 5 | False positives erode trust | A smoke alarm that fires at toast gets unplugged. | ⭐ TS 4.1 · Knowledge 3 |
| 6 | Switch off a noisy category (for now) | Take one alarm offline while you fix its sensor. | ⭐ TS 4.1 · Skill 2 |
| 7 | Role + reason in the system prompt | Tell the new hire who they are and why the rule exists. | 📘 docs |

**Vague vs explicit** (this lab's pull request)

| # | Instruction | False positives | What happened |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | “Check that comments are accurate” | 1 | A correct but old-looking comment flagged |
| 2 | “Be conservative, high-confidence only” | 5 | Style, naming and a house pattern all reported |
| 3 | ⭐ Report: bugs, security, comments that contradict code · Skip: style, naming, local patterns | 0 | Only the 4 real issues |
| 4 | Severity “very serious / serious” | — | Identical bugs rated differently |
| 5 | ⭐ Severity with a code example per level | — | Identical bugs rated the same |
howItWorks:
1. **Give a role and a reason:** who reviews, and who reads the findings (docs: context helps Claude generalise).
2. **List what to report** as categories: bugs, security, comments that contradict the code.
3. **List what to skip:** style, naming, patterns the codebase already uses.
4. **Define severity** with one concrete code example per level.
5. **Watch dismissal rates.** A category developers keep dismissing gets switched off until its criteria are rewritten.

labIntro:
You write a code reviewer's **system prompt** and choose which categories are switched off. The **simulated** reviewer reads
the prompt and reviews one pull request whose true issues are known: 4 real issues in the report categories, 1 real
performance issue, and 9 look-alikes. The lab measures **precision** (how many findings are real), **recall** (how many real
issues were found) and **severity consistency**.

variants.label: ✅ ⭐ explicit Report/Skip criteria · severity with examples · noisy category off
variants.code:
from utils.review_lab import review   # SIMULATED code reviewer on a pull request with known true issues

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You review pull requests for a payments team.
Report only: bugs (wrong results, crashes), security issues, performance problems with measurable impact, and comments
whose claimed behaviour contradicts what the code actually does.
Skip: style and formatting, naming preferences, and local patterns this codebase already uses consistently.
Severity:
- critical: exploitable or loses data, e.g. SQL built from user input.
- major: a wrong result in normal use, e.g. an off-by-one that drops the last item.
- minor: wrong only in rare edge cases, e.g. a date bug at midnight on a DST change."""

# developers dismissed 4 of 5 performance findings last sprint -> off while its criteria are rewritten
DISABLED = ["performance"]

review(SYSTEM_PROMPT, DISABLED)
variants.observe: Every scenario: reported c2 (comment contradicts the code), b1 and b2 (off-by-ones) and s1 (SQL injection) — precision 100%, recall 100%, both off-by-ones “major”. The one real performance issue (p1) is “not checked” while that category is switched off.
variants.why: The reviewer is told exactly what counts, what doesn't, and what each severity looks like — like a new colleague given a clear brief.

variants.label: ⭐❌ A — “check that comments are accurate”
variants.code:
from utils.review_lab import review   # SIMULATED code reviewer on a pull request with known true issues

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You review pull requests for a payments team.
Report only: bugs (wrong results, crashes), security issues, performance problems with measurable impact, and comments -
check that comments are accurate.
Skip: style and formatting, naming preferences, and local patterns this codebase already uses consistently.
Severity:
- critical: exploitable or loses data, e.g. SQL built from user input.
- major: a wrong result in normal use, e.g. an off-by-one that drops the last item.
- minor: wrong only in rare edge cases, e.g. a date bug at midnight on a DST change."""

# developers dismissed 4 of 5 performance findings last sprint -> off while its criteria are rewritten
DISABLED = ["performance"]

review(SYSTEM_PROMPT, DISABLED)
variants.observe: The old-looking comment at cart.py:12 is flagged (c1) although the code does what it says — precision 80%.
variants.why: “Accurate” is vague; “flag only when the claimed behaviour contradicts the code” is a criterion the reviewer can apply.
variants.fix: Say what counts: a contradiction between comment and code.

variants.label: ⭐❌ B — “be conservative: only report high-confidence findings”
variants.code:
from utils.review_lab import review   # SIMULATED code reviewer on a pull request with known true issues

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You review pull requests for a payments team.
Be conservative: only report high-confidence findings.
Severity:
- critical: exploitable or loses data, e.g. SQL built from user input.
- major: a wrong result in normal use, e.g. an off-by-one that drops the last item.
- minor: wrong only in rare edge cases, e.g. a date bug at midnight on a DST change."""

# developers dismissed 4 of 5 performance findings last sprint -> off while its criteria are rewritten
DISABLED = ["performance"]

review(SYSTEM_PROMPT, DISABLED)
variants.observe: Style (y1–y3), a local pattern (l1) and the correct comment (c1) are all reported — 5 false positives, precision 44%.
variants.why: The reviewer is confident about style nits; confidence isn't the filter — categories are.

variants.label: ⭐❌ C — severity levels without examples
variants.code:
from utils.review_lab import review   # SIMULATED code reviewer on a pull request with known true issues

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You review pull requests for a payments team.
Report only: bugs (wrong results, crashes), security issues, performance problems with measurable impact, and comments
whose claimed behaviour contradicts what the code actually does.
Skip: style and formatting, naming preferences, and local patterns this codebase already uses consistently.
Severity:
- critical: very serious.
- major: serious.
- minor: not very serious."""

# developers dismissed 4 of 5 performance findings last sprint -> off while its criteria are rewritten
DISABLED = ["performance"]

review(SYSTEM_PROMPT, DISABLED)
variants.observe: Two identical off-by-one bugs come back as “major” and “minor”.
variants.why: “Serious / very serious” can't be applied consistently; a concrete code example per level can.

variants.label: ⭐❌ D — leaving the noisy category on
variants.code:
from utils.review_lab import review   # SIMULATED code reviewer on a pull request with known true issues

SYSTEM_PROMPT = """You review pull requests for a payments team.
Report only: bugs (wrong results, crashes), security issues, performance problems with measurable impact, and comments
whose claimed behaviour contradicts what the code actually does.
Skip: style and formatting, naming preferences, and local patterns this codebase already uses consistently.
Severity:
- critical: exploitable or loses data, e.g. SQL built from user input.
- major: a wrong result in normal use, e.g. an off-by-one that drops the last item.
- minor: wrong only in rare edge cases, e.g. a date bug at midnight on a DST change."""

# developers dismissed 4 of 5 performance findings last sprint -> off while its criteria are rewritten
DISABLED = []   # WRONG: the category developers keep dismissing stays on

review(SYSTEM_PROMPT, DISABLED)
variants.observe: Performance adds p1 (real) and p2–p5 (dismissed) — precision falls to 56%.
variants.why: A category developers keep dismissing teaches them to ignore every finding, including the accurate ones.
variants.fix: Switch it off while its criteria are rewritten; switch it back on when they're precise.

questions.q: Your CI reviewer flags about 40 code comments a week as “inaccurate” when they are merely old-fashioned but still true, and developers now dismiss most of its comment findings. The prompt says “check that comments are accurate”. What is the best change?
opts: Add “be careful and only flag comments you are sure about” to the existing comment instruction.
Replace it with an explicit criterion: flag a comment only when its claim contradicts what the code does.
Remove comment checking from the reviewer entirely, since comments are too subjective for an automated review.
Cap the reviewer at five comment findings per pull request, so that the false positives are fewer.
questions.explain: An explicit criterion says exactly what counts as a problem, which removes the ambiguity behind the false positives. A is a vague confidence instruction, which doesn't improve precision. C throws away a useful check. D cuts real and false findings alike.

questions.q: A reviewer's prompt says “be conservative and only report issues you're highly confident about”, yet 55% of its findings are style nits or speculative concerns that developers dismiss. Adding “be even more conservative” last month changed nothing measurable. What will improve precision most?
opts: Ask the reviewer to attach a confidence score to each finding, and report only those scored 9 or 10.
Run the reviewer twice on each PR, and keep only the findings that appear in both independent runs.
Name the categories to report (bugs, security) and those to skip (minor style, accepted local patterns).
Switch to a larger model, which will interpret “conservative” more consistently across all of its reviews.
questions.explain: General instructions such as “be conservative” don't improve precision; specific report and skip categories do. A relies on self-reported confidence, which is poorly calibrated. B suppresses real findings that only show up intermittently. D hopes a bigger model will resolve an ambiguity the prompt created.

questions.q: Developers dismiss about 80% of the reviewer's “performance” findings. A survey shows they now also skim past its security findings, although those are right 90% of the time. Rewriting the performance criteria properly will take about three weeks. What is the best immediate step?
opts: Temporarily disable the performance category while its criteria are rewritten, so trust recovers.
Keep every category, but add a note to each performance finding saying these are often false positives.
Mark security findings in bold red, so developers notice them among the noisy performance findings.
Keep performance findings, but move them to the end of each review, after all the security findings.
questions.explain: A high false-positive category erodes trust in the accurate ones. Disabling it while its criteria are fixed restores trust straight away. B and D keep the noise in front of developers. C treats the symptom, and developers who distrust the tool will skim past red text as well.

questions.q: Two identical unchecked-null bugs in different files come back as “critical” in one review and “minor” in another. Over a month, 30% of findings changed severity when the same PR was re-reviewed. The prompt lists the four severity names with no further detail. Which change gives consistent classification?
opts: Lower the temperature to zero, so the reviewer gives the same severity each time it sees similar code.
Remove the severity field and report every finding at one level, so there is nothing to disagree about.
Run a second reviewer that re-grades each finding's severity, and keep the higher of the two grades.
Define each severity level in the prompt, with concrete code examples of what belongs at that level.
questions.explain: Severity names without definitions leave the boundary to chance. Explicit criteria with code examples for each level make classification consistent. A may make repeat runs more alike, but it doesn't fix an undefined boundary between different code. B removes useful information. C adds a second undefined judgement.

questions.q: The team deliberately catches broad exceptions in its plugin loader, a documented local pattern. The CI reviewer flags it on every pull request that touches the loader, about 12 a week, and developers now reflexively dismiss all exception-handling findings, including real ones. What is the best prompt change?
opts: Tell the reviewer to skip every exception-handling finding, since developers dismiss them all anyway.
State that this local pattern is accepted and should be skipped, while real exception bugs are reported.
Add “use good judgement about exception handling” to the reviewer's instructions for the plugin loader.
Exclude the plugin loader's directory from review entirely, so that none of its code is checked any more.
questions.explain: Explicit criteria include what not to report: here, an accepted local pattern. Real issues stay in scope. A throws away real findings. C is a vague instruction. D stops reviewing the loader altogether.

faq.q: Isn't “only report high-confidence findings” a reasonable safety net?
faq.a: It feels like one, but the guide's point is that it doesn't improve precision. The model can be confident about a style nit. Categories say what's in and out.

faq.q: Does switching a category off mean losing real issues?
faq.a: For a while, yes. In the lab, one real performance issue goes unchecked. The guide treats it as temporary: restore trust, fix that category's criteria, then switch it back on.
In the system prompt. The docs say even one sentence of role focuses Claude's behaviour, and explaining why a rule exists helps it generalise.
